title: Loop Lighting
description: Loop lighting creates a small nose shadow that loops toward the corner of the mouth and does not connect to the cheek shadow. The key sits slightly off axis and a little high, a middle step between butterfly and Rembrandt.

sections.title: Narrative function

blocks.text: The face is shaped but still friendly: interviews, earnest close-ups, people we are supposed to trust. You get a hint of cheek shadow and a definite nose, without the painterly triangle or the glamour butterfly.
It is the wrong tool when you need a mask of light and dark, or a fashion-symmetric face. If that loop grows until it joins the cheek, you have crossed into Rembrandt.
If you center the key, you are back at butterfly.

sections.title: How it works

blocks.text: Offset the key about 30 to 45 degrees from the nose, slightly above eye line, softness medium so the loop is a clean comma, not a smear. Fill can sit opposite at a gentle ratio (2:1 to 4:1).
Color is usually the room: window daylight or soft tungsten. The shadow-side cheek still receives some light; that is the difference from Rembrandt.
Prompt: Loop lighting on [Subject], key slightly off-axis, a small loop shadow from the nose toward the corner of the mouth.

sections.title: When to use it

blocks.text: Use it for a natural portrait that is still shaped, an interview, a two-shot that should not look lit. Do not use it when you want a cheek triangle or a half-face cut.

sections.title: Compared with similar shots

blocks.text: Rembrandt lighting connects nose shadow to cheek shadow and leaves a triangle. Butterfly lighting is on axis with a philtrum butterfly.
Split lighting goes to 90 degrees and drops the far cheek. Bounce will wrap the loop away if the source gets too large.
Motivated lighting may produce a loop from a slightly off window, but the pattern is the geometry, not the justification.

sections.title: In film

blocks.text: Interview cinematography and news-adjacent films such as Frost/Nixon live on loop because both eyes stay open and the face still has a side. The Social Network's talking-head grammar often sits here: slightly off keys, not painterly triangles.

sections.title: Prompt it

blocks.text: Name the loop and forbid the triangle. Use: "Loop lighting on [Subject], key slightly off-axis, a small loop shadow from the nose toward the corner of the mouth." Add that the loop does not touch the cheek shadow.

sections.title: What usually goes wrong

blocks.text: The usual wrong cousin is Rembrandt or butterfly. The tell is a connected cheek triangle, or a perfectly centered under-nose butterfly.
Fix it by offsetting the key a little and stopping before the shadows merge.

sections.title: Questions

blocks.text: What is loop lighting in film?
A slightly off-axis key that throws a small loop-shaped nose shadow toward the mouth corner. That shadow does not join the cheek shadow.
Loop lighting vs Rembrandt lighting
Loop leaves a gap between nose shadow and cheek shadow. Rembrandt joins them, creating a triangle of light on the far cheek.
When should I use loop lighting?
Use it for a natural, still-shaped portrait or interview. Skip it when you want glamour symmetry or a dramatic cheek triangle.
How do I prompt loop lighting for AI image or video?
Put the key slightly off axis. Specify a small loop shadow from the nose toward the mouth that does not connect to the cheek shadow.
